content: Your doctor has prescribed antihemophilic factor (recombinant) to assist your blood in clotting. This medication will be administered either by direct injection into your vein or through an intravenous fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter over approximately 5 to 10 minutes. The frequency of administration may vary, ranging from two to three times daily to once every two or more weeks, depending on your specific needs. Antihemophilic factor (recombinant) is a synthetic version of substances naturally produced by the body. It works by activating clotting factors in your blood to form clots and reduce bleeding episodes. In some cases, this medication may be prescribed for other uses. If you have questions about its use, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Your healthcare provider may monitor the effectiveness and potential side effects of your treatment through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your symptoms respond to the medication. Precautions Before Administration: Inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have ever had a reaction to antihemophilic factor or if you are allergic to any drugs, including prednisone, cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan), cyclosporine (Neoral, Sandimmune), heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin (Lovenox, Normiflo), interferon alfa (Roferon-A, Intron), vincristine (Oncovin), vitamin K, or other vitamins. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking this medication, contact your doctor immediately. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking antihemophilic factor (recombinant) before any procedures. Administering Your Medication: Before administering antihemophilic factor (recombinant), inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or check the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution, but show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your medication instructions precisely. Do not stop your therapy on your own for any reason, and do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical problem, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your healthcare provider immediately to resume your therapy. Side Effects: Minor Side Effects: Antihemophilic factor (recombinant) may cause minor side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if any of the following symptoms are severe or persistent: Dizziness Headache Sore throat Itching Upset stomach Vomiting Fatigue Severe Side Effects: If you experience any of the following symptoms, stop the infusion and contact your healthcare provider immediately: Increased pulse rate Hives Unusual bleeding or bruising Difficulty breathing Chest discomfort or tightness Chills Fever If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Storing Your Medication: Your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days’ worth of antihemophilic factor (recombinant) at a time. You will be instructed on how to prepare each dose. Store your medication as directed, and ensure you understand the proper storage requirements. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and store all medications and supplies out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will provide instructions on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In Case of Emergency or Overdose: In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 or your local emergency services immediately. Signs of Infection: If you are receiving antihemophilic factor (recombinant) through a vein or under your skin, it is important to recognize the symptoms of a catheter-related infection (an infection at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin).
